articles.title: Australia’s trade surplus jumps to A$2.8 billion, a seven-month high, on LNG and metals
articles.desc: A stronger trade surplus is modestly supportive for the Australian dollar, reinforcing the currency’s link to commodity prices. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. Th
articles.content: A stronger trade surplus is modestly supportive for the Australian dollar, reinforcing the currency’s link to commodity prices. With energy prices elevated by the Middle East conflict, Australia is better placed than many importers, as LNG and coal export earnings help cushion a rising fuel bill. The data are unlikely to shift Reserve Bank of Australia expectations on their own, given the volatile gold component. Traders will look to upcoming volume data for a cleaner read on how much net exports are adding to growth. -- Gas and metals did the heavy lifting for Australia’s trade surplus in September, with a big drop in gold imports doing the rest. Summary: Australia’s goods trade surplus widened to about A$2.8 billion in September, the largest in seven months That was up from A$184 million in August and well above forecasts Exports rose 2.3% from the month before, led by other mineral fuels, including LNG, and metals Imports fell 3.3%, driven by a nearly 35% drop in gold imports Higher fuel prices have yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill Australia’s goods trade surplus widened sharply in September to its largest in seven months, as a rise in exports of liquefied natural gas and metals coincided with a steep fall in gold imports, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday. The surplus on goods trade came in at about A$2.8 billion (around US$2 billion), up from A$184 million in August and well ahead of forecasts for a surplus of roughly A$1 billion or less. Exports rose 2.3% from the previous month, following a 3.7% gain in August. The increase was driven by other mineral fuels, a category that includes liquefied natural gas, and by metals, highlighting the support Australia’s resource sector continues to draw from global commodity demand. Imports fell 3.3%, reversing a 5.8% rise in August. The decline was led by gold, where imports dropped by nearly 35%. Gold flows can be volatile from month to month and often swing the headline balance, so the scale of the drop flatters the underlying improvement to some degree. The figures also suggest the recent rebound in fuel prices has yet to show up meaningfully in the import bill. As a large importer of refined fuel, Australia’s import costs would be expected to rise if higher prices persist, which could narrow the surplus in coming months. At the same time, higher energy prices tend to cut both ways for Australia. As a major exporter of liquefied natural gas and coal, the country benefits from elevated global energy prices on the export side, partly offsetting the cost of more expensive fuel imports. The stronger trade position is a positive for the economy’s external accounts, though its contribution to growth will depend on how the volume of trade, rather than its value, develops over the quarter. Attention now turns to whether commodity export strength can be sustained, and how quickly rising fuel costs feed into imports. Both will shape whether September proves a high point for the surplus or the start of a firmer trend. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: France considers easing citizenship rules for retirees with foreign pensions
articles.desc: France's interior ministry may issue flexible guidelines for citizenship requests from retirees with foreign pensions, addressing concerns over income origin and integration criteria.
articles.content: France considers easing citizenship rules for retirees with foreign pensions Ministry looks to ease foreign income citizenship hurdles Calls for more flexible guidance to be issued to prefectures with regard to French citizenship requests from retirees with foreign pensions French universal vehicle tax mooted to offset falling fuel revenues How will Thursday’s strikes impact drivers in France? UK-EU deal could ease rules on pets, cheese and British sausages France’s interior ministry has told senators it is to consider issuing more flexible guidelines to with regard to French citizenship requests from retirees with foreign pensions. was joined by Nièvre senators Patrice Joly and Nadia Sollogoub for a meeting at the ministry. This comes as there have been increasing reports, including by readers, of retirees being refused on the sole basis that their income comes mostly from abroad. being told in a circular sent by former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau last year to reject such applications on grounds that the person has not totally transferred the centre of their interests to France – though it said exceptions could be made. Ms Bonnefoy said: “Together with several of my fellow senators, I met with the office of the interior minister [Laurent Nuñez] to raise the difficulties in accessing naturalisation, notably for retired foreign nationals but also for students. “We were able to draw the ministry’s attention specifically to the effects of the tightening of rules introduced by the May 2025 circular, which is being applied too rigidly in many departments and is leading to frequent refusals based on the foreign origin of income. “This discussion offered a glimpse of positive developments. Several avenues were raised so as to relax the criteria currently being used, notably taking into account a person’s civic commitment or the overall financial circumstances of applicants. "The ministry has undertaken to provide us with a prompt written response.” , Ms Bonnefoy said more students are now being refused, as the circular had demanded that applicants should show proven and lasting integration through work as well as stable and sufficient income. This makes success difficult for those pursuing studies or recently out of university, she said. Another reader refused explicitly because his income is mostly from UK pensions, Rob Gill, wrote to Ms Bonnefoy after reading our articles. “She wrote a very nice email back, saying she thought I had a very good case,” he said. She suggested, among other points, contacting the Gisti foreigners’ rights association for its advice, which gave the view that once a case reaches the Nantes administrative court, it is hard to win unless you can prove an error was made. However, the first avenue is to send an appeal to the interior ministry for a review (via the same website they applied on) and Mr Gill, 73, from Charente-Maritime, is now looking for a lawyer to help in wording this. The retired civil servant and tax expert said: “I have a bit of investment income, some from French sources, but if the rule on foreign income is all that counts, I’m bound to fail. “We’ve been here 10 years and I am chair of a cultural association, I’m on the committee of my bridge club, I was responsible for safeguarding a listed building that was threatened with collapse, and I have a French language degree.” It is unclear so far if a new circular goes out, if this will help those already refused. However, in case of a refusal, it is possible to reapply from scratch, if you consider your situation has improved. articles.title: Butler to appear before Senate GOIC today
articles.desc: Main focus: Insurance coverage that allegedly protects $10Mil investment By Asi Andrew Fa'asau andrew@samoanews.com Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate Government Operations Investigative Committee (GOIC) is scheduled to hear testimony this morning from Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula's Executive
articles.content: Main focus: Insurance coverage that allegedly protects $10Mil investment By Asi Andrew Fa'asau andrew@samoanews.com Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Senate Government Operations Investigative Committee (GOIC) is scheduled to hear testimony this morning from Governor Pulaali'i Nikolao Pula's Executive Advisor on Finance, Brett Butler, as lawmakers continue their investigation into the controversial $10.1 million investment of American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) interest earnings. Committee members are seeking answers regarding insurance coverage that administration officials have repeatedly stated was obtained to protect the investment. Specifically, senators want details concerning the amount allegedly paid for the insurance, the date the payment was made, and any documentation supporting the transaction. According to the committee's request, Butler is expected to provide records and clarify the circumstances surrounding the insurance arrangement, which has become a central issue in the Senate's ongoing inquiry into the investment. Lawmakers are also seeking clarification of comments made recently by Governor Pulaali'i during a press conference, where he suggested that senators may have been questioning the wrong parties regarding the insurance coverage. The Governor's remarks came after representatives of Trade and Merchant Trade Services and Southern Pacific Insurance Company appeared before the committee and denied having any direct contractual relationship with the American Samoa Government concerning the investment. During that hearing, company representatives testified that they had not directly dealt with ASG and had not issued an insurance policy guaranteeing the return of the Territory's $10.1 million investment. Those statements appeared to conflict with earlier testimony from administration officials who told lawmakers that the investment had been insured. Asked about the discrepancy during his press conference, Governor Pulaali'i responded that "the Fono had talked to the wrong people." Butler subsequently attempted to explain the arrangement, stating that the insurance protection was not purchased directly by ASG from Southern Pacific Insurance or Trade and Merchant Trade Services. Instead, according to Butler, the insurance was part of a broader structure involving McKinley Beech Tree (MBT), the entity connected to the investment transaction. He explained that ASG's funds were not to be released until there was an insurance mechanism in place to protect the investment. According to Butler, MBT retained the services of an insurance broker known as First Gate, which in turn worked with Trade and Merchant Trade Services. Trade and Merchant then allegedly arranged for Southern Pacific Insurance Company to act as an insurer or guarantor associated with the transaction. Under that explanation, MBT worked through its broker to coordinate the coverage, while Trade and Merchant and Southern Pacific Insurance provided the financial backing for the arrangement. However, the exact nature of the relationship among those entities, and what protection was actually provided, remains unclear and is expected to be a major focus of Wednesday's hearing. In addition to seeking proof of any insurance payments, senators want Butler to explain the specific roles played by each of the companies mentioned throughout the investigation, including MBT, First Gate, Trade and Merchant Trade Services, and Southern Pacific Insurance Company. Committee members have indicated that they are attempting to establish a clear chain of responsibility and determine whether the insurance arrangement described by administration officials is the same arrangement discussed by representatives of the off-island companies. The hearing is expected to be closely watched because it follows testimony by company officials that has raised new questions about the existence, scope, and beneficiaries of any insurance coverage associated with the $10.1 million investment. Senators have stated that obtaining a definitive explanation of the insurance arrangement is critical to determining whether adequate safeguards were in place to protect public funds before the investment was made. Section: Local News Tags: Senate GOIC

Hardeman with his wife Lizzie Davis and their home on Cason Street. J. G Hardeman was in the Funeral Business in 1891, that business eventually became Casey Funeral Home. His obituary follows. HENDERSON, Dec. 18, 1943 — Funeral services will be held at the family residence on Cason St. Sunday afternoon at three o’clock for J. G. Hardeman, 76, the oldest merchant in Chester county who died Thursday. Mr. Hardeman was born in Henderson county, his father having moved there in 1884. Having graduated from West Tennessee Christian College, he taught school for one session in Shelbina, Missouri, and also about a year at Medon. He entered the hardware business in 1891 and continued active in the business until about two weeks before his passing. In 1894, he married Miss Lizzie Davis. To them, three children have been born: Robert D. Hardeman, who has continued with his father in business for about thirty years; Netha Hardeman, who died in Denver, Colo., about twenty-five years ago; and Jasper Hardeman. He also leaves a brother T. B. Hardeman of Memphis, who has passed the four-score mark. There are two sisters, Mrs. Ben McIntyre of Jackson and Mrs. L. L. Brigance of Henderson. Mr. Hardeman has been a member of the Church of Christ from early manhood and has served as an elder for a long number of years. He has also been a member of the Board of Directors of Freed-Hardeman College since its foundation and has been one of its chief advisors and supporters in every way. © Copyright 2026 Chester County Independent Powered by Creative Circle Media Solutions

articles.content: Eurocamp just announced a major change to its Spain holiday parks - The Mirror Eurocamp just announced a major change to its Spain holiday parks Eurocamp has announced a major change affecting its popular Spain holiday parks from 2026 but it could be good news for Brits looking for a sunny getaway parks (or parcs, as they call them) are already a firm favourite with Brits looking for cheap and cheerful getaways in the summer, with sites across plenty of popular destinations including France, Italy and Spain. Now, the holidays giant has announced it will be making a major change to a number of its , in what could be good news for holidaymakers. That's because for the first time ever, Eurocamp is going to be offering winter sun holidays, kicking off in 2026. While typically Eurocamp sites close for the winter, this year there will be three parcs remaining open throughout the colder months; in Costa Dorada (home to Salou), with prices from £452 per party during the quieter seasons. It marks the first time that Brits can opt for Eurocamp breaks in Spain during Christmas, or even for February half term. However, they're not the only destinations on offer. Eurocamp already has sites in the French Alps which are open during the ski season, as well as its location which is popular with Brits hoping to visit the French capital for its Christmas markets. It's not the only brand to offer up holiday parks during the winter months. For example, has a number of sites in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, including one park just a stone's throw away from Disneyland Paris. For Brits who are after winter sun but don't want to commit to jet-setting off to far-flung Caribbean islands, Spain and its islands can be an ideal compromise. In fact, the popular country has 8 of Europe's 10 sunniest cities according to research from travel pros at Holidu. Cities such as Cordoba or Malaga, in the southern part of Spain, are where you'll likely have more luck given temperatures average 19C in November, while Barcelona keeps a balmy 15C although it does get cooler in the evenings. are famed for their year-round sunshine, and can enjoy temperatures of up to 23C as late as early December. So while it may not be warm enough for swimming in the sea, it's still pleasant enough that you can enjoy the outdoors whether you wander along the bustling promenades, or want a lunch al fresco. (Not to mention the cooler mornings are ideal for those who want to kick off the day with a hike around those volcanic landscapes). articles.title: ‘You Don’t Put Your Head in the Sand for 4 Years’: Colossal CEO Ben Lamm on Working With Trump
articles.desc: The company’s cofounder recently convinced the Trump administration to support an initiative to gather DNA samples from endangered species.
articles.content: ‘You Don’t Put Your Head in the Sand for 4 Years’: Colossal CEO Ben Lamm on Working With Trump | WIRED CEO and cofounder Ben Lamm: “They like technology, they like to make money, they like to save money—and they also really like to take exciting wins.” That’s how Colossal convinced an administration that hasn’t exactly been friendly to conserving land and wildlife to support an initiative to gather DNA samples from endangered species on Wednesday. Lamm’s company has garnered plenty of press for and creating wooly mice using gene editing as part of a greater effort to revive the wooly mammoth. Colossal raised $230 million in its Series C last year at a valuation of $10.2 billion. The company is looking to raise a new round that would value it at between $20 billion and $30 billion, according to earlier this year. The startup has spun out multiple companies, including one that uses microbes to destroy plastic. Colossal also has a , a startup Lamm developed with Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey that plans to create genetically enhanced dogs for the military, law enforcement, and first responders. But it’s the biobanking efforts that Lamm says are more important as climate change and habitat destruction puts more pressure on wildlife. (Lamm said the company is using a similar approach with Warhound with the goal of reducing dependence on what he called “puppy mills” churning out working dogs in Europe.) Colossal has been criticized by conservationists for distracting from efforts to protect endangered species. Promising to de-extinct species in the future could increase the odds of policies today that lead more animals to go extinct, a criticism that was leveled when Colossal began working with the Trump administration earlier this year on its biobank. Lamm defended the company’s effort, saying that the dire forecasts for biodiversity mean “you don’t put your head in the sand” for four years. Colossal has also come under fire from critics for overselling its results. The genome of the dire wolves Colossal created, for example, is very similar to gray wolves. Critics say the company’s announcements of bringing back these and other creatures are more style than substance. At the time of the , Clemson University professor David Jachowski told WIRED that there’s “inherently some subjectivity” when it comes to defining species. The company is also going to miss its initial 2028 deadline for creating a wooly mammoth, though Lamm said Colossal has made headway with 130 edits to mammoth genes. He said he’s fine if you want to call the company’s creations gene-edited gray wolves or any future wooly mammoths Colossal creates “hairy elephants.” While Colossal has made plenty of splashy announcements, Lamm said the company has “undersold” its gene-editing efforts and that there will be more “surprise and delight moments for the world.” One thing that’s not coming, though, is working on extinct ocean predators like the megalodon. While Lamm said the company has received plenty of interest about a meg, it’s not happening. Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond is a senior editor for WIRED’s science section. He has covered climate, weather, and energy for nearly 15 years. Prior to WIRED, he ran climate tech coverage for Bloomberg, where he edited award-winning journalism and ran the flagship newsletter. He takes out his phone and quickly searches for “auto repair shops near me.” Your shop comes up. He taps the listing and notices that your shop is only open until 5 p.m., when in fact it’s open until 6. Adam calls the phone number to double-check whether you’re still open, but no one picks up. He is already moving on to the next shop on the list. Adam doesn't leave a voicemail or an angry review, so you never hear about him. If the information on your listing isn't correct or up to date, you're losing customers. Google says customers are 2.7 times more likely to consider a business reputable when they find a complete profile, and 70% more likely to visit. But there's actually a detail that most shop owners miss. Google lets users to a business's details, so your hours, phone number, and even your category can change without you touching them. Google that users suggested roughly 80 million updates to business hours, contact details, and other information across Maps in 2025. Google may send an email or display an alert on your dashboard to let you know about a suggested edit, but sometimes such alerts are easily forgettable when you're running a busy shop. You have four days to accept or reject the changes. Once those four days pass, Google may publish the changes automatically if other public information, like your website, supports them. You don’t have to spend hours on this. Just set aside 10 minutes once a month to go through your Google Business Profile. Make sure your hours, holiday hours, phone number, and category are all updated. Also keep an eye on your email so you’ll know if any changes have been suggested. About 73% of consumers began their most recent , according to a 2026 BrightLocal survey. Your customers should be able to easily find the services you offer, price estimates, timing, and an online booking form. Slow loading, a lot of pinching and zooming to see details, and copying your phone number by hand are inconveniences that are likely to prompt a customer to close the tab without a second thought. Open up your website on your phone right now. Can you find your hours, your services, a tap-to-call button, and a way to book without scrolling too far down? If not, these need to go on your to-do list immediately. You can also ask family, friends, and staff to go through the website and point out any issues they find. 3. There’s no online form or booking option Plenty of people look for a repair shop at 9 p.m., long after you've closed. And while the phone is still the most popular way to reach a business, in March 2025, prefer it for customer service, which means about two-thirds would rather reach you another way. A booking form gives these customers an easy way to reach you, even after hours. articles.title: Astronomers hunting for aliens find new way to work out when they would contact us
articles.desc: Work uses game theory to try and understand when would be the right time to
articles.content: Astronomers hunting for aliens find new way to work out when they would contact us | The Independent Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Astronomers hunting for aliens and trying a new technique to work out exactly when they would contact us. The research uses ideas from game theory to predict not just where extraterrestrial civilisations would message us from, but when they would do so. Institute, a non-profit that searches for alien life – is based on the idea that we would not only need to point our telescopes at the right part of space to pick up messages from aliens. We would also need to be listening at the right time, to avoid missing it. The work is based on the idea of the “Schelling point”, an idea from game theory based on working out the choice that two parties would make independently, without being able to co-ordinate. Two people who had decided to meet up in New York City but were unable to get in contact with each other might choose to meet in Grand Central Station at noon, for instance, since that is likely to be chosen separately by the other person without being able to co-ordinate. The scientists are looking for a similar place and time for contact from alien civilisations. They have focused their work on the anti-solar point, a specific part of the sky that another alien world might choose on its own. The new work did not yet pick up any signals from alien intelligence. But it already offers a breakthrough: it represents both the first observational search of that part of space, as well as a potential start of a new approach for hunting for alien life that could one day pick up such signals. To choose the right part of space, astronomers borrowed an idea that we have already used to find distant planets. When a world passes in front of its star, observers can see it in a process called a “transit”, which briefly dims the light from that star and shows not only that the planet exists but also can be used to understand its orbit and where it is in relation to its star. To an alien civilisation doing the same sort of work with Earth, our planet would also be right between them and our Sun. From Earth, the planet would appear in the complete opposite direction from the Sun, which is known as the anti-solar point. That means that both we and any theoretical alien civilisation that was observing us would be able to pick a specific part of space, without being able to communicate, and so could each independently recognise that alignment. It could therefore be a useful way of co-ordinating communication without already being able to send messages to each other. The scientists note that there is nothing to suggest that an alien civilisation would choose to use this point, or certainly that they are already doing so. But it offers a new way to think about how we try and search through space for aliens, they said. “The challenge in SETI isn’t simply deciding where to point a telescope,” said , SETI Institute research scientist and co-lead author of the paper. “It’s figuring out where and when another civilisation might choose to transmit. The anti-solar point gives us a way to think about that problem from the perspective of a potential sender, rather than just the receiver.” Usually, SETI searches pick a particularly exciting star, or the planetary systems around them. The new research takes a new route, not picking a specific target but instead looking using a particular alignment that might also be worked out by those distant worlds. Researchers are already trying out the theory using the SETI Institute’s Allen Telescope Array (ATA) at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in Northern California. articles.title: Helium Health secures $2.5 million Google grant to tackle maternal deaths with AI
articles.desc: Helium Health has received $2.5 million grant from Google.org to deploy AI tools that help identify pregnancy risks and improve maternal healthcare delivery in Nigeria.
articles.content: Helium Health secures $2.5 million Google grant to tackle maternal deaths with AI Helium Health secures $2.5 million Google grant to tackle maternal deaths with AI Helium Health, a Nigerian healthtech startup, has secured a ₦3.4 billion ($2.5 million) grant from Google.org, tech giant Google’s philanthropic arm, to deploy artificial intelligence (AI) tools that help identify pregnancy risks and improve maternal healthcare delivery in Nigeria. The funding will support the rollout of HeliumMum, the company’s maternal health initiative that aims to reach 1.9 million pregnant women over three years. The programme will begin in Lagos, the initiative’s operational base, before expanding to Delta, Kano, and Oyo states. , and Helium Health hopes its AI-powered intervention will help address this burden by identifying pregnancy complications earlier and connecting women to appropriate care, and contribute to a 30% reduction in maternal mortality. “For the past decade, Helium Health has been building the technology and partnerships needed to improve healthcare delivery across Africa,” Dimeji Sofowora, Helium Health’s chief executive officer, said in a statement. “Through our maternal health initiatives, we’ve already reached over 3.5 million women, and Google.org’s support gives us an opportunity to build on that foundation, scale what works, and reach even more women with quality maternal healthcare.” The grant comes three months after Adegoke Olubusi, Helium Health’s co-founder and CEO, after nearly a decade, handing leadership to Sofowora, another co-founder who assumed the role in August. The leadership change followed the departure of another co-founder, Tito Ovia, in 2022, leaving Sofowora as the last founding team member actively involved in leading the business. Helium Health was the only Nigerian organisation selected among 15 recipients of Google.org’s $30 million Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation , announced in September 2026. The challenge supports organisations working with governments to use AI to improve public services, including healthcare. The funding will finance the deployment of AI-powered clinical decision-support tools within primary maternal healthcare services. Through HeliumMum, the company wants to help community health workers identify potential pregnancy complications earlier and connect expectant mothers to appropriate healthcare providers. The system will combine AI-driven risk detection with electronic medical records and clinical decision-support tools used by healthcare providers. Helium Health says it has already reached more than 3.5 million women through its maternal health initiatives. With the Google.org funding, it wants to reach another 1.9 million. The company will also receive technical support from Google engineers and AI product experts through a dedicated Google.org Accelerator. “AI holds incredible potential to transform public services, but there is often a gap between promise and practice,” said Maggie Johnson, Global Head of Google.org. “By equipping the 15 selected organisations with funding and pro bono support from Google’s own AI experts, we are empowering the people closest to the problem to show what is truly possible. Together, we can ensure that AI makes a profound, positive difference in the everyday lives of communities worldwide.” Founded in 2014 by Olubusi, Sofowora, and Ovia, Helium Health started by building electronic medical records and hospital management software to help healthcare providers digitise patient records. Over time, the company expanded and began offering tools for medical records, billing, practice management, and healthcare financing. In June 2023, Helium Health funding round led by AXA IM Alts, bringing its disclosed funding at the time to about $40 million.
